corpus.source: github.com/tae2089/context-diary, local checkout at commit 1054ca6, captured 2026-08-10
corpus.note: Built with `ccg build .` at the repository root; its own .ccg.yaml excludes tests and docs. Unlike gorm and cobra, this corpus carries real ccg annotations — 84 @intent/@domainRule lines written by the project's author — so it is the first external corpus that exercises the question path: intent retrieval, the CanAnswer gate, and reason-matched evidence. The identifier path is covered too, but the questions are the point.

authorship.written_by: assistant, 2026-08-10, before running any measurement; every judged symbol and file was verified to exist in the built graph first
authorship.caveat: Same rules as the primary set: expectations are never edited to make a run pass. The questions paraphrase what a developer would ask; they were written while reading the annotations, so vocabulary overlap with @intent text is real but not verbatim.

queries.why: The exact name of the HMAC check; a developer typing it wants the function.
Exact method name; the one place the bot writes its PR comment.
Exact method name; the batch persistence path.
The bare name is ambiguous in general but unique in this graph; the prepare-commit-msg hook body.
Two words naming package and function; the bare-mirror maintenance entry point.
Package plus function; the message validator that both the hook and CI call.
The feature spans the CLI command and the git line-history walker it joins; either file is a place to start. The mcptool explain handler is reachable from both.
One file implements the command that lists commits still lacking context.

queries.query: why is the commit never blocked by the hook
queries.why: hook.go records the never-block rule (I-1): every failure path warns to stderr and returns. main.go records the same rule at the git entry points: prepare-commit-msg always exits 0.

queries.query: how does the server verify a webhook really came from github
queries.why: github.go holds the HMAC check itself (authenticate before any side effect); serve.go records the ordering rule — verified before any parsing, invalid signature is 401.

queries.query: what happens when the ingest queue is full
queries.why: queue.go records the back-pressure signal on Enqueue; serve.go records the visible behavior — a full queue returns 503 with no side effects.

queries.query: how do korean searches find inflected words
queries.why: The domain rule on Store.Search: free text matches when either the tsvector FTS query or an all-words trigram substring hits, so agglutinative-language stems find their inflected forms.

queries.query: why does a rescan reindex commits that did not change
queries.why: store.go records force=true rebuilding derived children even when content is unchanged, so parser upgrades reach already-indexed commits; index.go records that --rescan ignores the cursor for exactly that reason.

queries.query: does the installer overwrite hooks that belong to another tool
queries.why: The install rule (I-3): never edit files it does not own — a foreign hook is left untouched and returned as a manual instruction.

queries.query: why does a merged pull request get acknowledged before indexing finishes
queries.why: The webhook handler's rule: a merged PR is enqueued and answered 202 immediately; ingestion runs in the background so the 10-second webhook timeout is never a factor.

queries.query: how does a crash avoid skipping or duplicating commits
queries.why: store.go records the atomic batch-plus-cursor guarantee on SaveEntries; gitlog.go records the fallback — an unreachable cursor triggers a full rescan, safe because inserts are idempotent.

queries.query: why does the bot keep only one comment per pull request
queries.why: UpsertComment's intent line: exactly one bot comment per PR so pushes never spam the thread.

queries.query: how are github app tokens refreshed
queries.why: AppAuth's intent: provide a valid installation token to every call, hiding the JWT exchange and hourly rotation.
The project has no deployment logic at all; nothing in the graph or the recorded reasons concerns rollouts. The right answer is nothing.
